Title: GPU-friendly surface model for Monte-Carlo detector simulations
Text:
GPU-friendly surface model for Monte-Carlo detector sim-
ulations
Severin Diederichs1,∗, Andrei Gheata1, Juan Gonzalez Caminero1, and Guilherme Lima2
1CERN, Geneva, Switzerland
2Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, IL, USA
Abstract. The demands for Monte-Carlo simulation are drastically increasing
with the Large Hadron Collider’s high-luminosity upgrade, and are expected
to exceed the currently available compute resources. At the same time, mod-
ern high-performance computing has adopted powerful hardware accelerators,
particularly GPUs. The AdePT and Celeritas projects aim to address the de-
manding computational needs by leveraging these heterogeneous computing
architectures. While both have successfully ported realistic detector simula-
tions to GPUs using the VecGeom library, the complexity of geometry modeling
emerged as a bottleneck. Thread divergence and high register usage were de-
grading the GPU performance. Therefore, a new, GPU-friendly surface-based
model has been introduced in the VecGeom library that decomposes the diver-
gent code of the 3D primitive solids into simpler and more balanced surface
algorithms. In this work, we present the latest developments, focusing on the
additions required to efficiently model complex setups like the CMS Phase-2
geometry. This includes memory reduction techniques, and adding accelerating
structures for faster traversal.
1 Introduction
The upcoming upgrade to the high-luminosity LHC at CERN present significant computa-
tional challenges for the full-detector Monte-Carlo simulations, driven by the need for in-
creased simulation throughput [1]. At the same time, the landscape of high-performance
computing is shifting towards heterogeneous architectures that rely on accelerators, primar-
ily graphics processing units (GPUs) [2]. Consequently, offloading parts of the simulation
workload to GPUs within Geant4 [3], the state-of-the-art detector simulation toolkit for the
LHC experiments, has become an active area of research and development. Two projects,
AdePT [4] and Celeritas [5], are currently exploring GPU acceleration for the transport of
the electromagnetic particles: electrons, positrons, and gamma particles. While initial per-
formance results are promising, the geometry modeling has been identified as a bottleneck in
both projects.
In general, geometry modeling is considered a performance-critical component of parti-
cle transport simulations. Contrary to graphics problems, these simulations require handling
hierarchical information, touching volumes, and navigation accuracy to a level that makes tes-
sellations prohibitive. Initially, both GPU projects relied on the solid model in the VecGeom

library [6] to model realistic setups. Although VecGeom’s solid model has a CUDA backend,
it was originally designed for vectorized CPU computation. Without GPUs as the original
target, the implementation has certain characteristics that limit the performance on GPUs.
High algorithm complexity and recursive function calls lead to a high register usage, while
the drastically different complexity among the different solid algorithms (i.e., computing a
box is fast and simple, computing a polyhedron with many sections is slower and complex)
leads to significant divergence. To overcome these performance limitations on GPUs, a new
surface-based geometry model was developed within VecGeom [7], having as rationale in-
creasing GPU friendliness by making geometry algorithms simpler and more uniform. The
surface model demonstrated promising initial performance results in simple test calorimeter
geometries. However, it did not yet support full LHC detector geometries.
In this paper, we give an update on the development progress for the VecGeom surface
model, including the additions implemented to support the full LHC detector geometries.
After a brief description of the model in Sec. 2, the latest developments are discussed in
Sec. 3, before providing a conclusion and an outlook on the future evolution of the model in
Sec. 4.
2 Description of the surface model
The VecGeom Surface model was first introduced in Ref. [7]. Since that description is still
accurate, only those features relevant to the latest development are described in this section.
The surface model aims to provide a GPU-friendly geometry implementation while al-
lowing seamless integration into the existing VecGeom API. The model decomposes the sup-
ported primitive 3D solids into a small set of surface types, reducing divergence across dif-
ferent types. At the same time, the per-surface algorithms generally have lower complexity
compared to their solid-based counterparts, reducing register usage in geometry navigation
— a potential limiting factor for GPU occupancy. To facilitate the integration of the surface
model into existing applications, surfaces are constructed directly from the solid model dur-
ing initialization. Additionally, the interface for geometry navigation requires only minimal
modifications to use the surface model.
The VecGeom implementation of the surface model follows a framed surface approach:
each surface consists of an infinite half-space to define the surface representation and a frame
that describes its boundaries. At the same time, infinite half-space surfaces are de-duplicated
into "common surfaces". When a particle hits a common surface, it traverses to the oppo-
site side and is relocated to the correct volume, accounting for the possibility that multiple
volumes share the same common surface. Consequently, the traversal of a solid has to first
determine the distance to the next surface to be hit, and then relocate the particle to the cor-
rect volume across the surface. Additionally, the framed surface approach enables efficient
computation of the "isotropic safety", defined as the closest distance to any object along any
direction. This quantity can drastically accelerate the propagation in magnetic fields, as it
reduces the number of geometry queries needed for bent particle trajectories.
3 Latest Developments
3.1 Adding missing solids required by the LHC experiments
After the initial development phase of the surface model, the capability to run full LHC-
scale detector simulations was an important next target. To achieve this, the surface model
must be able to convert all solid types in the LHC detector geometries into surfaces. Support
was added for the following solids: polycones, simple extruded solids, generic trapezoids,

tori, and orbs. Previously, the only available surface types were the planar one and a subset
of second-order surfaces: cylindrical, conical, and spherical. The toroidal volumes used in
the CMS Phase 1 geometry required a new torus surface, and the generic trapezoids used
in ATLAS’ electromagnetic end-caps (EMEC) required hyperboloids. New algorithms for
surface intersection and safety calculations were implemented for both surface types. The
CMS geometry setups also use reflected volume placements, requiring dedicated support in
the surface model. With these additions, the surface model can process both CMS Phase 1
and 2 and the full ATLAS detector geometries.
3.2 Controlling the memory required by the surface model
Having implemented all solid types required for full LHC-scale detector simulations, another
crucial task was to reduce the memory footprint. The surface model requires more memory
than the solid model because there are many more objects to be created. As a simple example,
in the solid model, a box placement requires only 3 doubles (the extent in the 3 dimensions)
and 12 doubles for its 3D transformation (translation and rotation), so 15 doubles in total.
In the surface model, the box is decomposed into 6 planar surfaces, each of them having a
3D transformation, so 72 doubles in total. Since the LHC detectors have up to more than 10
million hierarchical volume placements (touchable volumes), the increased memory footprint
quickly grows too large for the limited GPU memory in the case of LHC setups.
The memory usage can now be controlled via the scene concept. Instead of fully ex-
panding all touchable volumes and enumerating them with a single index, highly replicated
volumes are placed only once in memory, and they define their local reference frame, which
we call scene. Scenes represent a logical volume sub-hierarchy, where touchable volumes are
stored directly in the scene reference frame and addressable via a single scene index. Scenes
can be composed in case they also contain replicated volumes, so in the global reference
frame, a volume touchable is represented by a tuple (n0, n1, ..., nm) of scene indices, where m
is the depth of the tuple. The complete state information for all touchable volumes is stored
in a compact navigation table providing direct access based on tuple indices.
This approach can drastically reduce the memory footprint in complex setups at the cost of
additional computation for composing scene touchable transformations. The optimal scene
decomposition is performed during initialization and can be constrained by the maximum
scene depth (a compile-time option) and the minimum number of touchable volumes per
scene, allowing to fine-tune the trade-off between memory usage and extra computation. On
the GPU, since memory is scarce and computation is fast, this is a viable way to reduce the
memory footprint of the surface model. Note that this concept also applies to the solid model
in case of memory constraints for very large geometry setups.
As a result, the memory footprint of the surface model for complex detectors such as
CMS can be reduced to a few hundred MB using a maximum tuple depth of m = 4. At the
same time, the conversion time is reduced to less than one minute for the tested geometries.

3.3 Accelerating structures for faster navigation
The navigation in complex geometries requires accelerating structures to mitigate the O(n)
complexity of the naive distance calculation approach, which can slow down dramatically the
simulation when the number of candidates to check is very large. This is especially important
for a surface-based approach, as there are many surfaces per solid, leading to a significantly
increased amount of candidates.

The surface model’s navigation interface has three main functions: ComputeStepAnd-
Hit to identify and find the distance to the next surface being hit, ComputeSafety to find
the isotropic safety, and RelocatePointIn, to locate the correct touchable volume behind the
surface being hit. For all these functions, acceleration mechanisms are employed for perfor-
mance optimization purposes.
To accelerate the search for the next surface to be hit and the safety computation, a bound-
ing volume hierarchy (BVH) [8] is used, which was adapted from the original BVH for the
solid model in VecGeom. A BVH is a tree structure that recursively partitions the 3D ob-
jects to be checked into bounding volumes, in most cases using axis-aligned bounding boxes
(AABBs). During traversal, the algorithm first tests the parent bounding volume, which is a
fast check that can be done in single precision, and then checks the child nodes only in case
the ray intersects their bounding box. Then, when the child nodes are not further partitioned,
the remaining candidates need to be tested for intersection, which is a more expensive check.
The tree structure evaluation has O(log n) scaling. Depending on the 3D-primitive complex-
ity and how balanced the tree can be constructed, the BVH yields different speedups over the
naive looper approach. For the surface mode BVH acceleration, the ray tracing performance
results of 10 million random rays for three geometries, namely CMS Phase 2, the CMS high-
granularity calorimeter (HGCAL) test beam setup, and the LHCb calorimeters, are shown in
Table 2. The BVH yields more than an order of magnitude speedup compared to the naive
loop approach for the complex CMS Phase 2 geometry.

The relocation in the surface model can also be costly in complex geometries. For exam-
ple, in the HGCAL test beam setup, there are volumes containing 800 child volumes, which
all share a common surface with the parent. Thus, the correct child volume among the 800
must be identified when a particle hits such a common surface. An adaptive 2D spatial grid
is used to accelerate the search among the surface candidates. In the previously mentioned
example, the number of candidates to be checked was reduced to 5. To further improve the

within another across the common surface. Thus, by checking the embeddedness among

4 Conclusion and Outlook
Modeling LHC-scale detector geometries is challenging on GPUs. The VecGeom surface
model has taken significant steps towards this ambitious goal. Although still under active
development, the surface model currently shows similar performance to the solid model on
geometries such as the HGCAL test beam setup and only slightly lower performance on full
LHC geometries such as the CMS Phase 2 detector. At the same time, it uses fewer regis-
ters and is written in a performance-portable way, opening new performance improvement
opportunities for GPU particle transport simulation libraries such as AdePT and Celeritas.
To further improve the performance, it is planned to leverage the fact that, unlike the solid
model, the surface model does not rely on small pushes to determine whether a particle has
entered a solid or not. While these small pushes prevent the usage of lower precision than
64-bit floating point ("double") precision in the solid model, the surface model can use the
lower precision of 32-bit floating point ("single") precision at least in some performance-
critical parts. Thus, a mixed precision mode is envisioned, where some parts are calculated
in the faster single precision (such as distance to a surface, safety), while other quantities are
kept in double precision (such as the position in global coordinates). Preliminary tests show
promising performance improvements but simultaneously maintaining the numerical stability
is challenging and subject to future work.
